lesson.title: Sometimes True: The Ordinary Case Behind Every Equation
lesson.summary: Learn that a conditional equation is true for exactly one value of the variable, the ordinary case behind nearly every equation solved so far, and see it placed alongside identities and contradictions.
lesson.body:
A conditional equation is a linear equation in one variable that is true for exactly one value of that variable and false for every other value. This is the ordinary, everyday case: essentially every equation solved earlier in this unit, from one-step equations through variables-on-both-sides problems, has been a conditional equation, which is exactly why solving them produced a single specific number for x rather than a true or false statement with no variable left. The name reflects that the equation's truth is conditional on x taking one particular value.

Solve 4x + 9 = 2x + 21 to see a conditional equation solved from start to finish. Subtract 2x from both sides: 2x + 9 = 21. Subtract 9 from both sides: 2x = 12. Divide both sides by 2: x = 6. Unlike an identity or a contradiction, the variable did not cancel out here; the coefficients of x on the two sides, 4 and 2, were different, which is exactly what allowed a single value of x to be isolated. Check by substituting x = 6 into the original equation: the left side is 4(6) + 9 = 24 + 9 = 33, and the right side is 2(6) + 21 = 12 + 21 = 33. Both sides equal 33, confirming x = 6 is the one and only solution.

A second quick example confirms the pattern: solve 9x - 2 = 4x + 23. Subtract 4x from both sides to get 5x - 2 = 23, add 2 to both sides to get 5x = 25, then divide by 5 to get x = 5. Checking gives a left side of 9(5) - 2 = 43 and a right side of 4(5) + 23 = 43, matching, and again the coefficients of x, 9 and 4, were different from the start, which is why a single solution emerged.

The reason this equation resolved to a single answer, while the identity and contradiction examples elsewhere in this unit did not, comes down to the coefficients of x on each side. Whenever those coefficients are different, as 4 and 2 are here, subtracting one from the other during the variables-on-both-sides step leaves a nonzero coefficient of x, and dividing by that nonzero number always produces exactly one value of x. It is only when both sides start with the identical coefficient of x that the variable cancels completely, opening the door to an identity or a contradiction instead.

In the language of a solution set, a conditional equation has a solution set containing exactly one number, here {6}, in contrast to the empty set of a contradiction or the set of all real numbers belonging to an identity. This is why a conditional equation feels the most natural: it matches the expectation that an equation should have one specific answer, and it is the case that word problems are almost always designed to produce, since a real situation usually has one specific number as its answer.

Together, identity, contradiction, and conditional equation cover every possible outcome for a linear equation in one variable: always true, never true, or true exactly once. Recognizing which of the three you are looking at, by checking whether the variable survives to the end and, if it does not, whether the leftover statement is true or false, completes the toolkit for confidently solving and interpreting any linear equation in this unit.
